claims.text: The damaged component is made from a nickel-based superalloy.
Traditional fusion welding of the nickel-based superalloy leads to hot cracking because of its physical and microstructural characteristics.
FSW tool rotational speeds of 300–600 rpm constitute an optimized processing range for this repair.
The FSW traverse speed can be selected to keep the peak temperature below the alloy's incipient melting point.
A peak processing temperature below 1050°C is an appropriate sub-melting boundary for the unspecified nickel-based superalloy.
An inert atmosphere will minimize oxidation during the repair.
FSW will form an ultrafine-grained stirred zone.
FSW will refine the γ and γ′ phases in the stirred zone.
Severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization cause the proposed grain and phase refinement.
FSW joins the material in the solid state and therefore eliminates formation of a liquefied zone.
Eliminating the liquefied zone avoids the hot cracking associated with fusion welding.
FSW repair under the proposed conditions will produce a defect-free joint.
The FSW-repaired joint will be mechanically robust and retain the original component's service properties under high temperature and high stress.
The FSW-repaired joint will outperform a traditional fusion-welded repair under aggressive service conditions.
Traditional fusion-welded repairs typically suffer hot cracking and compromised performance under aggressive service conditions.
